questions.stem:
Statement I: The government has recently announced a 30% hike in fuel prices.
Statement II: Public transport ridership has increased by 25% in the past month.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: Unrelated events (wrong: higher fuel prices logically cause more people to use public transport)
I is the cause and II is the effect (correct: fuel price hike → more expensive driving → people switch to public transport ✓)
II is the cause and I is the effect (wrong: high ridership doesn't cause fuel price hikes)
Both are effects of a common cause (possible but the direct logical link between I and II is more compelling)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Causal chain: Fuel prices rise (I) → driving becomes more expensive → people switch to public transport → ridership increases (II). Statement I is the CAUSE; Statement II is the EFFECT. The link is logical and direct.

questions.stem:
Statement I: A leading pharmaceutical company has recalled 50,000 units of a blood pressure medication citing safety concerns.
Statement II: Sales of alternative blood pressure medications from competitor companies have risen by 40% this week.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: Both are causes of a third event (wrong: II is a consequence, not a co-cause)
Unrelated events (wrong: the recall logically leads to patients seeking alternatives)
I is the cause and II is the effect (correct: recall of medication → patients need alternatives → competitor sales rise ✓)
II is the cause and I is the effect (wrong: competitor sales rising doesn't cause a recall)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Recall of a medication (I) → patients who depended on it now seek alternatives → competitors' sales rise (II). I causes II. The timing ('this week' = right after the recall) reinforces the causal link.

questions.stem:
Statement I: There has been excessive rainfall in the region for the past two weeks.
Statement II: Several low-lying areas of the city are experiencing severe flooding.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: Both are causes of a common effect (wrong: II is an effect, not another cause)
I is the cause and II is the effect (correct: excessive rainfall (I) → flooding in low-lying areas (II) ✓)
II is the cause and I is the effect (wrong: flooding doesn't cause rainfall)
Unrelated events (wrong: clearly related — rainfall causes flooding)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Excessive rainfall (I) → water accumulates → low-lying areas flood (II). Clear cause-and-effect: I causes II. Natural causation is straightforward.

questions.stem:
Statement I: A new metro rail line connecting two major business districts was inaugurated last month.
Statement II: Traffic congestion on the parallel highway has reduced by 30%.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: Unrelated events (wrong: new metro → fewer people driving → less congestion)
I is the cause and II is the effect (correct: new metro provides an alternative → some drivers switch → highway congestion drops ✓)
II is the cause and I is the effect (wrong: reduced congestion doesn't cause metro inauguration)
Both are effects of a third cause (possible but the direct causal link is stronger)

questions.explanation: B is correct. New metro line (I) → commuters have a public transport alternative → fewer cars on the parallel highway → traffic reduces (II). The timing ('last month') and the parallel route make the causal link compelling.

questions.stem:
Statement I: A major university in the city has started offering free online courses in data science.
Statement II: The unemployment rate among technology graduates in the city has fallen by 10%.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: I is definitely the cause and II is the effect (wrong: unemployment fall could have many causes; the link is possible but not certain)
Both are effects of the same cause (possible: a strong economy could cause both course availability and employment)

The cause-effect relationship is plausible but requires more evidence to establish definitively (correct: free courses COULD help graduates get jobs, but correlation ≠ causation; timing and magnitude matter ✓)
Completely unrelated events (wrong: there is a plausible causal pathway)

questions.explanation: C is correct. While there IS a plausible link (free courses → more skilled graduates → better employment), we cannot definitively say I caused II without more evidence. The unemployment fall could be due to many factors (new companies, economic growth). This question tests CRITICAL reasoning about causation vs correlation.

questions.stem:
Statement I: The central bank has raised interest rates by 0.5% to combat inflation.
Statement II: The stock market indices have fallen by 3% since last week.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: Unrelated events (wrong: interest rate hikes typically affect stock markets)
I is the cause and II is the effect (correct: interest rate hike (I) → borrowing costs rise → corporate profitability expected to fall → investors sell stocks → stock indices fall (II) ✓)
II is the cause and I is the effect (wrong: stock markets falling doesn't cause rate hikes)
Both effects of a common cause (possible but the direct causal chain from I to II is well-established in economics)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Interest rate hike (I) → investors anticipate reduced corporate earnings due to higher borrowing costs → sell shares → stock indices fall (II). This causal chain is well-established in economics. Rate hikes are a known 'negative signal' for equity markets.

questions.stem:
Statement I: A popular social media platform announced new privacy-restricting policies.
Statement II: Rival social media platforms have seen a surge in new user registrations.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: Unrelated (wrong: users disliking new privacy policies logically move to alternatives)
II is the cause and I is the effect (wrong: new users joining rivals doesn't cause the original platform to restrict privacy)
I is the cause and II is the effect (correct: privacy-restricting policies (I) → users leave/avoid the platform → join rival platforms → rivals see surge (II) ✓)
Both caused by a third common cause (no clear common external cause evident)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Privacy restrictions (I) → users concerned about privacy migrate to rivals → rivals gain users (II). This is a direct competitive displacement effect. Users leaving one platform directly adds users to alternatives.

questions.stem:
Statement I: Scientists have discovered a highly effective vaccine against a new disease.
Statement II: Global stock markets have risen by 5% following the announcement.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: Unrelated (wrong: vaccine discoveries affect healthcare companies and market sentiment)
I is the cause and II is the effect (correct: vaccine discovery (I) → optimism about controlling disease → positive market sentiment → stocks rise (II) ✓)
II is the cause and I is the effect (wrong: stock market rise doesn't cause scientific discoveries)
Both effects of a common cause (unlikely; the scientific discovery preceded and triggered the market reaction)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Vaccine discovery (I) → markets interpret this as positive news (disease will be controlled, economic disruption will end) → investor confidence rises → markets rise (II). Medical breakthroughs regularly trigger positive market movements.

questions.stem:
Statement I: Several employees at a food processing plant have fallen ill.
Statement II: The factory has been temporarily shut down for inspection.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: II is the cause and I is the effect (wrong: the factory shutdown couldn't cause the illness if the shutdown came AFTER the illness)
I is the cause and II is the effect (correct: employees falling ill (I) → authorities investigate → factory shut for inspection (II) ✓)
Unrelated (wrong: clearly connected — illness triggers inspection)
Both effects of a common cause (wrong: the illness directly led to the shutdown; no separate common cause needed)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Employee illness (I) → public health/regulatory concern → authorities order factory shutdown for investigation (II). The illness is the cause; the shutdown is the regulatory response. Timing: illness comes first, shutdown follows.

questions.stem:
Statement I: There has been a significant drop in the prices of solar panels globally.
Statement II: The adoption of solar energy by households and businesses has increased dramatically.

Are these two statements:

options.option_text: II is the cause and I is the effect (possible: high demand could reduce prices through economies of scale, but typically price drop comes first)
I is the cause and II is the effect (correct: price drop (I) → solar becomes more affordable → more households/businesses adopt it (II) ✓)
Both are effects of a common cause (possible: technological advancement could reduce prices and increase adoption simultaneously)
Unrelated events (wrong: price and adoption of the same product are clearly related)

questions.explanation: B is correct. When prices of solar panels fall (I), solar energy becomes economically viable for more people → adoption increases (II). This is classic price elasticity: lower price → higher demand → more adoption. I causes II.
